prompt.context: Our client, Potato Inc., is a producer of fried potato crisps (chips). The product is high in sodium and fat and comes in several flavors (plain, barbecue, etc.). Customers are loyal 18-to-30-year-old males who mostly reside in the Southern United States. The year is 2010. The client makes and manufactures chips domestically and has two main product lines: premium and price-value. They sell through convenience stores, gas stations, drug stores, and supermarkets. Recently, profits have been decreasing.
prompt.question: Potato Inc. would like to understand why profits are decreasing and what to do about it.

clarifying_info.q: Has revenue changed? Are customers buying less?
clarifying_info.a: Customers are buying the same volume of product as before — total units sold have not declined.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have a specific profitability target?
clarifying_info.a: No, they are just looking to be as profitable as possible given the circumstances.

exhibits.title: Cost Breakdown 2005–2010
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing Potato Inc.'s cost structure as a percentage of total costs from 2005 to 2010, broken down into four categories: Logistics, Labor, COGS, and PPE.
exhibits.data: Annual stacked bars from 2005 to 2010; cost components are Logistics, Labor, COGS, and PPE; total always sums to 100%; the chart reveals how each cost component's share has shifted over the six-year period.

framework: Revenues: price × quantity — examine whether price or mix has shifted across premium vs. price-value lines
Costs: break down into COGS, Labor, Logistics, PPE — identify which buckets are growing as a share of revenue
Industry/macro context: 2010 post-recession environment — consumer trade-down behavior
Product mix: shift from higher-margin premium to lower-margin price-value products
Cost-reduction levers: labor (outsourcing, automation, training/efficiency), logistics, procurement

questions.prompt: Phase 1 — What might be happening in the industry to explain declining profits, given that total volume sold is unchanged?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize the 2010 post-recession context and hypothesize that consumers are trading down from the premium product line to the price-value line. Since revenue = price × quantity, flat quantity combined with a mix shift toward cheaper (lower-margin) products reduces both average selling price and profit per unit sold. The higher-margin premium line loses share, compressing overall profitability even with stable volumes.

questions.prompt: Phase 2 — After reviewing the cost exhibit, what cost-cutting opportunities do you see, and what are the risks?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe from the exhibit that Labor costs have been rising as a share of total costs over 2005–2010. Key opportunities: (1) Outsource production to reduce labor costs; (2) Automate labor-intensive processes; (3) Improve efficiency through training or quality control. Risks to flag: (1) Loss of in-house expertise / knowledge retention; (2) Potential increase in logistics costs if production moves offshore or to a new location; (3) Execution lead time — restructuring takes time and has transition costs. Candidate should acknowledge these risks and suggest mitigation strategies (e.g., phased outsourcing, keep core processes in-house, negotiate logistics contracts).

brainstorming.prompt: How can Potato Inc. improve profitability?

categories.name: Revenue levers
ideas: Incentivize consumers to trade back up to the premium line (promotions, limited-edition flavors)
Introduce a new premium SKU to justify higher price points
Expand distribution channels beyond current retail footprint
Target new customer segments beyond 18–30 Southern males

categories.name: Cost reduction — Labor
ideas: Outsource part of production to lower-cost providers
Improve workforce efficiency through training and quality control programs

categories.name: Cost reduction — Logistics
ideas: Consolidate suppliers or negotiate volume discounts
Improve demand forecasting to reduce over-production and waste

categories.name: Cost reduction — COGS/Procurement
ideas: Renegotiate potato and oil supply contracts
Explore alternative lower-cost raw material suppliers

categories.name: Cost reduction — PPE
ideas: Sell and lease back underutilized equipment
Increase utilization of existing plant capacity to spread fixed costs

recommendation: Profits are declining primarily because customers are trading down from the higher-margin premium line to the price-value line in the post-recession environment — volume is flat but mix has shifted unfavorably.
On the cost side, labor is the rising cost component and should be addressed through a combination of outsourcing non-core production and investing in automation.
risks: Trade-down trend may persist or deepen if the economy recovers slowly
Outsourcing risks expertise loss and potential logistics cost increases
Automation requires upfront capital investment with a longer payback period
next_steps: Analyze exact margin differential between premium and price-value lines to quantify the mix-shift impact
Conduct a detailed labor cost benchmarking study to identify the best outsourcing or automation option
Develop a consumer incentive plan (e.g., promotions or loyalty program) to migrate price-value customers back to the premium line as the economy recovers
